title: Proverbs
subtitle: A father's teaching, Wisdom's call, and the sayings of the wise
lead: Proverbs is Israel's book of wisdom for ordinary life. It opens with a heading, "The proverbs of Solomon son of David, king of Israel" (1:1), and a statement of purpose: the sayings are for "knowing wisdom and discipline" (1:2), to give the naive shrewdness and a young man knowledge and discretion (1:4). Then it names its foundation in one line: "The fear of the LORD is where knowledge begins" (1:7). Wisdom here is not cleverness but skill in living: how to speak, work, handle money, choose friends, treat the poor, govern, marry and stay faithful, all under the eye of the LORD.

The book is a collection of collections, each with its own heading. Chapters 1–9 are a long introduction: a father's talks to his son, warnings against the gang of robbers and the "strange woman," and the speeches of Wisdom herself, pictured as a woman who calls in the streets, who was with the LORD before the world was made (8:22–31), and who builds a house and spreads a feast (9:1–6). Then come hundreds of short two-line sayings credited to Solomon (10:1–22:16), "the words of the wise" (22:17–24:22), a short appendix (24:23–34), the proverbs that Hezekiah's men copied (25–29), the words of Agur (30) and of King Lemuel, whose mother taught him (31:1–9), and a closing alphabet poem in praise of "a woman of strength" (31:10–31).

Proverbs was read in Israel's homes and schools, and it shaped Jewish and Christian teaching from the start. The rabbis heard Wisdom's voice as the voice of the Torah; the New Testament quotes the book on discipline, humility and kindness to enemies; and the church fathers argued for a century over what Wisdom's words in chapter 8 mean for Christ. Its sayings are blunt and memorable, and they often state how life usually goes rather than what always happens. Read together, they teach a reader to see two roads, the road of wisdom and life and the road of folly and death, and to choose the first.
facts: The headings name Solomon (1:1; 10:1; 25:1), unnamed "wise" teachers (22:17; 24:23), Agur son of Jakeh (30:1) and King Lemuel, who passes on his mother's teaching (31:1). Chapters 25–29 were copied by "the men of Hezekiah king of Judah" (25:1). The Talmud says that Hezekiah and his company wrote down Proverbs (Bavli Bava Batra 15a). Most scholars see the book as an anthology gathered over several centuries, with Solomon as the patron of the tradition rather than the writer of every line.

The sayings in 10–29 are often thought to go back to the time of the kings (about 950–700 BC), and 25:1 ties one collection to Hezekiah (about 715–687 BC). Chapters 1–9 are usually dated later, to the Persian or early Greek period (about 500–300 BC), and many think they were written as the introduction when the book took its final shape. Traditional readers date most of the book to Solomon (about 970–930 BC).

Israel and Judah under the kings, and later Judea after the exile. The world of the book is the town gate, the market, the field, the household and the royal court. Kings appear often; the Temple, the priests and Israel's history almost never do.

Wisdom literature: instructions from a parent or teacher to a "son" (1–9; 22:17–24:22; 31:1–9), speeches by Wisdom as a woman (1:20–33; 8; 9), two-line sayings (10–29), numerical sayings (30) and an acrostic poem (31:10–31). Almost all of it is Hebrew poetry built on parallel lines.
Hebrew, with a few rare words, and in 31:2 the Aramaic word bar, "son." The Greek translation, made in Egypt in the 200s or 100s BC, is very free and puts chapters 24–31 in a different order.

In Jewish Bibles it is one of the Writings, usually after Psalms and Job; Psalms, Proverbs and Job form the three poetic books whose Hebrew accents differ from the rest. In Christian Bibles it stands among the poetic or wisdom books, after Psalms and before Ecclesiastes.
authorship: Jewish and Christian tradition credits the book to Solomon, whose wisdom 1 Kings 4 describes: "Three thousand proverbs came from his lips" (1 Kings 4:32). On this view Solomon composed or gathered chapters 1–24, Hezekiah's scribes copied more of his sayings about two centuries later (25:1), and Agur and Lemuel were real teachers whose words were added at the end. Rabbinic tradition held that Solomon wrote the Song of Songs in his youth, Proverbs in his middle years and Ecclesiastes in old age (Song of Songs Rabbah 1:1). Some conservative scholars today, such as Bruce Waltke, defend Solomon's authorship of much of the book, including chapters 1–9, pointing to the book's headings and to Egyptian instructions of a similar shape from the second millennium BC.

Most scholars read the headings as the book's own record that it grew in stages. The two-line sayings of 10:1–22:16 and 25–29 are usually thought to be the oldest material, drawn from the family, the village and the royal court of the monarchy. The section 22:17–24:22 draws on the Egyptian Instruction of Amenemope. Chapters 1–9, with their long poems and their figure of Wisdom, are usually dated to the Persian or early Hellenistic period and seen as the work of the editors who put the book together; some find ties to Deuteronomy and to the worries of Judea after the exile (Toy; McKane; Fox; Clifford). On this view Solomon's name stands at the head because he was Israel's model sage.

Many scholars hold that a real tradition of court wisdom goes back to Solomon's time, as it did in Egypt, even if the book was finished much later. They take the headings seriously as a history of collection: older sayings, credited to Solomon, kept and enlarged by scribes under later kings and edited after the exile (Murphy; Longman; Whybray).

audience.to: In the book's own voice, a "son": a young man being taught by his father and mother (1:8; 4:1–4; 31:1), or a pupil addressed by his teacher. He is about to marry, to do business, to stand at the town gate and perhaps to serve a king. Wisdom also calls to "the naive" and to every human being (8:4–5), so the book is open to anyone willing to learn. The finished book was read by Judeans after the exile who had no king of their own and had to keep faith in daily life.
audience.why: To form character: to make the young wise before the world tempts them, to teach them to fear the LORD, to guard their speech, work hard, treat the poor fairly, avoid violence and adultery, and to see that the choices of daily life lead either to life or to death. The editors put the father's talks and Wisdom's speeches first so that the reader would come to the short sayings already committed to Wisdom.
views: Some scholars think many of the short sayings began as folk proverbs of the village and the household, passed on by parents and elders, like proverbs in Africa and elsewhere (Westermann; Golka). The book's "my son" and its mention of the mother's teaching (1:8; 6:20) fit this setting.

Others think the sayings were gathered and taught in a school for royal officials, as in Egypt, where instructions were written for future scribes and courtiers; the many sayings about kings and the heading at 25:1 support this (Lemaire).

Others place the book among scribes who learned to read and write by copying and memorizing texts like these, so that the "son" is a pupil and the "father" a teacher (Carr; Crenshaw). The book's polish and its use of the Egyptian Amenemope point to trained writers.

Many think chapters 1–9 and the closing poem were written when the book was finished in Persian-period Judea, to teach young men loyalty to their families and their community. Some connect the warnings about the "foreign woman" with the debate over marriage to outsiders in Ezra 9–10 and Nehemiah 13 (Blenkinsopp; Washington; Camp).

outline: Title and purpose; the fear of the LORD is where knowledge begins
The father warns his son against the gang that kills for gain
Wisdom calls in the street and warns those who refuse her
Seek wisdom like silver; it will save you from evil men and the strange woman
Trust the LORD, honor him and accept his discipline
Happy is the one who finds wisdom; deal fairly with your neighbor
A father's own father's teaching; the two roads; guard your heart
The strange woman's honey; drink from your own well
Pledges, the ant, the troublemaker and seven things the LORD hates
Teaching as a lamp; the fire of adultery
Wisdom your sister; the young man and the woman at dusk
Wisdom's great speech: her worth, her rule, her place before creation
Two feasts: Wisdom's house and Woman Folly's
The proverbs of Solomon, first half: the righteous and the wicked, the wise and the fool
The proverbs of Solomon, second half: the LORD's plans, kings, speech and wealth
The words of the wise: thirty sayings, many close to the Egyptian Amenemope
More sayings of the wise; the field of the lazy one
The proverbs of Solomon copied by Hezekiah's men
The words of Agur: a sage's doubt, a prayer, and numerical sayings
The words of King Lemuel, taught by his mother
An alphabet poem: the woman of strength

lenses.name: History and setting
lenses.desc: Reads the sayings in the settings the book itself names: Solomon's court, where wisdom was prized and traded with Egypt and Sheba (1 Kings 4:29–34; 10:1–9), the scribes of King Hezekiah (25:1), the household where a father and mother teach a son (1:8; 4:3–4), the town gate where elders judge, and the foreign sages Agur and Lemuel. It asks what each saying meant for a farmer, a merchant, a courtier or a young husband in ancient Israel.

lenses.name: Critical
lenses.desc: Asks how the book's collections were made, dated and joined; why chapters 1–9 look later than the short sayings; how 22:17–24:22 uses the Egyptian Instruction of Amenemope; how the Hebrew text compares with the Greek translation, whose order and additions differ, and with the Syriac, the Targum and the Dead Sea Scrolls; and how scholars read the female figures of Wisdom, Folly and the strange woman.

lenses.name: Ancient wisdom
lenses.desc: Sets the sayings beside the wisdom writings of Israel's neighbors: the Egyptian instructions of Ptahhotep, Any and Amenemope, in which a father teaches his son; the Sumerian Instructions of Shuruppak and the Babylonian Counsels of Wisdom; and the Aramaic sayings of Ahiqar. It also looks at the goddesses of wisdom and order, such as Egypt's Maat, whom some scholars compare with Lady Wisdom.

lenses.name: Jewish tradition
lenses.desc: How the rabbis, the Targum and Jewish commentators read Proverbs: Wisdom as the Torah, through which God created the world (Genesis Rabbah 1:1); the tree of life as the Torah (3:18); the strange woman as heresy or idolatry; the woman of strength sung at the Friday-night table; and the commentaries of Rashi, Ibn Ezra, Gersonides, Meiri and Malbim.

lenses.name: Christian
lenses.desc: How the New Testament quotes and echoes Proverbs (Hebrews 12:5–6; James 4:6; 1 Peter 4:18; 1 Peter 5:5; Romans 12:20), and how the churches read it: Christ as the Wisdom of God (1 Corinthians 1:24), the debate over Proverbs 8:22 at the time of the Council of Nicaea, Wisdom's feast as a picture of the Eucharist and the Church, and the book's long use in moral teaching, from the fathers to the Reformers and modern preachers.

sections.b:
The text page beside each chapter can show several translations. Only the one you pick is loaded.

Plain English

A fresh rendering made for this site from the Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex), at about an 8th-grade reading level. Each verse was drafted from a word-by-word gloss of the Hebrew, then checked against other English versions and redrafted wherever it followed one of them too closely. Many proverbs are known by heart in older wording; the Plain keeps familiar wording only where the Hebrew forces it. Proverbs is poetry: the Plain keeps one verse per line, marks the poetic lines with slashes, and keeps each saying's two lines short and parallel. Headings in chapters 1–9 mark each talk or speech; in the short-saying collections they mark groups of related sayings.

Key terms

The book uses a cluster of words for wisdom and folly, and the Plain renders each the same way throughout unless a note says otherwise. Chokmah is "wisdom" ("Wisdom" when she speaks as a woman); musar is "discipline"; binah and tevunah are "understanding" (tevunah is "discernment" where both stand in one verse); da'at is "knowledge"; 'ormah is "shrewdness"; mezimmah is "discretion" in a good sense and "schemes" in a bad one; tushiyyah is "sound wisdom." The fools are the kesil, "fool"; the 'evil, "stubborn fool"; the nabal, "godless fool"; the lets, "mocker"; and the peti, "the naive." Tsaddiq and rasha' are "righteous" and "wicked." The 'ishshah zarah of chapters 2, 5 and 7 is "the strange woman," and nokhriyyah, "the foreign woman." Yir'at YHWH is "the fear of the LORD" (see the note at 1:7). Hesed is "loyal love," She'ol is left as "Sheol," and a parent's torah is "teaching."

The text and the versions

The Plain follows the Leningrad Codex, and its Ketiv and Qere readings are noted where they matter. The Greek is cited from Swete's edition of Codex Vaticanus with its notes on Codex Sinaiticus, Codex Alexandrinus and Codex Ephraemi, and the critical text of Rahlfs where it differs; the readings of Aquila, Symmachus and Theodotion, the Syriac, the Targum and Jerome's Latin are given as reported by Toy and other commentators. The Dead Sea Scroll fragments of Proverbs are cited as reported in their official edition.

Other translations

The Berean Standard Bible, the King James Version, the American Standard Version, Young's Literal Translation and the World English Bible can be shown for comparison.

sections.h: The headings and how the book was put together
sections.b:
Proverbs tells the reader how it was made. Seven headings divide it:

  • 1:1 "The proverbs of Solomon son of David, king of Israel": the title of the whole book, followed by its introduction (1–9).
  • 10:1 "The proverbs of Solomon": 375 two-line sayings to 22:16. The number 375 is the numerical value of the Hebrew letters of the name Solomon (Shelomoh), which may be deliberate.
  • 22:17 "The words of the wise": a teacher's instruction, with its "thirty sayings" (22:20), to 24:22.
  • 24:23 "These too are by the wise": a short appendix to 24:34.
  • 25:1 The proverbs of Solomon that "the men of Hezekiah king of Judah" copied out (25–29).
  • 30:1 "The words of Agur son of Jakeh."
  • 31:1 "The words of Lemuel, a king," taught by his mother; followed by the alphabet poem on the woman of strength (31:10–31), which has no heading of its own.

The headings show that the book is an anthology. Its parts differ in form: chapters 1–9 are long poems, most of 10–29 are single sayings set side by side, and chapter 30 is built on numbers. They also differ in mood: 10–15 sets the righteous against the wicked in almost every verse, while 16–22 and 25–29 say more about kings and about the LORD's hidden plans. Some sayings appear twice, in the same or nearly the same words (for example 14:12 and 16:25, or 18:8 and 26:22), as happens when collections made separately are joined.

The book has a frame. It begins with Wisdom as a woman who builds a house and calls the naive to her table (9:1–6), and it ends with a real woman who builds up her house and whose husband and children praise her (31:10–31). Its first and last words on wisdom both rest on the fear of the LORD (1:7; 31:30). Many scholars think the editors who wrote or placed chapters 1–9 also placed the closing poem, so that the reader enters through Wisdom's door and leaves with a picture of wisdom lived out in a household (Camp; Fox).

sections.h: Solomon and the other named authors
sections.b:
Solomon's name stands at the head of the book and of two collections. 1 Kings remembers him as the wisest of kings, wiser than the sages of Egypt and the East: "Three thousand proverbs came from his lips, and there were one thousand and five of his songs" (1 Kings 4:32). The queen of Sheba came to test him with riddles (1 Kings 10:1). The book's heading at 25:1 shows that later scribes still traced their sayings to him, and the Talmud credits the writing down of Proverbs to "Hezekiah and his company" (Bavli Bava Batra 15a).

Not all of the book claims to be Solomon's. "The words of the wise" (22:17; 24:23) come from unnamed teachers. Agur son of Jakeh (30:1) and Lemuel (31:1) appear nowhere else in the Bible. The word massa' beside their names can mean "oracle" or can be the name of Massa, an Arab tribe descended from Ishmael (Genesis 25:14), so they may have been foreign sages, as Job and his friends were foreign. Jewish tradition often took Agur and Lemuel as names of Solomon himself (Rashi on 30:1 and 31:1). See the notes on those verses.

Many modern scholars think the book's attribution to Solomon works the way Psalms' attribution to David does: it names the king who stood at the source of the tradition and in whose name wisdom was taught. Others hold that Solomon wrote the larger part of it himself. Both sides agree that the book was finished by scribes after his time.

The Greek translation of Proverbs, made in Egypt probably in the 200s or 100s BC, is one of the freest in the Greek Bible. Its translator wrote polished Greek, rewrote images, filled out the parallel lines, and often turned a saying toward a moral or religious lesson. It differs from the Hebrew in four large ways.

Order. In the Greek, after 24:22 come the first part of Agur's words (30:1–14), then the appendix of 24:23–34, then the rest of Agur (30:15–33), then Lemuel's mother's words (31:1–9), then the Hezekiah collection (25–29), and last the woman of strength (31:10–31). Swete's edition numbers this run as 24:24–77 and 29:28–49. The Greek has no names Agur or Lemuel; it turns 30:1 into "Fear my words, son" and 31:1 into "My words have been spoken by God."

Additions. The Greek has many lines that the Hebrew lacks. In chapters 1–9 they include a fuller 1:7, a verse on the bee beside the ant (6:8a–c), a call to honor the LORD in 7:1a, and three verses each after 9:12 and 9:18. Some of these may translate a Hebrew text different from the Masoretic Text; others are the translator's own or later scribes' work (Tov; Fox).

Omissions. The Greek leaves out a number of lines, such as 4:7, 8:29a–b and 8:32b–33; Codex Vaticanus also lacks 1:16.

Changes of sense. In 2:16–17 the strange woman becomes "evil counsel"; in 8:22 Wisdom says "The Lord created me"; in 25:1 the Hezekiah collection becomes "the miscellaneous instructions of Solomon." The New Testament quotes the Greek where it differs, at 3:12 (Hebrews 12:6), 3:34 (James 4:6; 1 Peter 5:5) and 11:31 (1 Peter 4:18).

Scholars disagree about how much of this goes back to a different Hebrew text. Tov argues that some of the larger differences reflect a different edition of the book; Cook stresses the translator's own Jewish and Hellenistic outlook; Fox's edition weighs each case. The notes on each verse name the Greek where it matters.

sections.h: Proverbs beside the wisdom of Egypt and Mesopotamia
sections.b:
Israel was not the only nation with sages. 1 Kings says that Solomon's wisdom went beyond "all Egypt's wisdom" (1 Kings 4:30), assuming that Egypt's was famous. Egyptian instructions from about 2400 to 600 BC, such as those of Ptahhotep, Any and Amenemope, are written as a father's or official's teaching to his son, like Proverbs 1–9 and 22:17–24:22. They praise silence and self-control, warn against the strange woman and against greed, and speak of a cosmic order, Maat, that rewards right conduct. Mesopotamia had the Sumerian Instructions of Shuruppak, the Babylonian Counsels of Wisdom and long lists of proverbs; the Aramaic sayings of Ahiqar circulated across the Persian empire.

The closest parallel is the Egyptian Instruction of Amenemope, published in 1923. In 1924 Adolf Erman showed that Proverbs 22:17–24:22 follows it closely in many places, including its thirty chapters (compare the "thirty sayings" of 22:20). Most scholars think the Hebrew writer adapted Amenemope, adding the LORD where the Egyptian named his gods. The notes in those chapters set the texts side by side and say what the parallel shows and what it does not.

Proverbs shares much with these writings but differs at the root: its wisdom begins with "the fear of the LORD" (1:7), the God of Israel, and its Wisdom is not a goddess but the LORD's own, "acquired" by him before the world began (8:22).

sections.h: Lady Wisdom, Woman Folly and the strange woman
sections.b:
Chapters 1–9 give wisdom and folly the shape of women. Wisdom shouts in the streets and at the gates (1:20–21; 8:1–3), says that she was with the LORD before the mountains and the deep (8:22–31), and invites the naive to a feast in her house of seven pillars (9:1–6). Woman Folly sits at her door and calls the same naive to stolen water and secret bread (9:13–18). Between them stands the "strange woman," another man's wife whose smooth words lead a young man to death (2:16–19; 5; 6:20–35; 7).

Readers have taken these figures in many ways. The rabbis heard in Wisdom's voice the Torah, through which God made the world (Genesis Rabbah 1:1), and in the strange woman heresy or idolatry. Christian writers from the New Testament on saw in Wisdom a picture of Christ, the Wisdom and Word of God (1 Corinthians 1:24; John 1:1–3), and argued over what her words "the LORD acquired me" (8:22) mean. Some modern scholars trace Wisdom to the goddesses of the ancient world; others see her as a bold poetic figure for the LORD's own skill and order in creation; others see her as drawn from the wise women and wives of Israel's households (Camp). Feminist scholars point out that the chapters speak only to young men and divide women into the wise and the dangerous, and ask what that teaches (Newsom; Yee). The chapter pages for 1, 2, 5, 7, 8 and 9 give these readings in detail.

Proverbs was read as Scripture before the time of Jesus. Ben Sira, about 180 BC, models his own book on it, and the New Testament quotes it as Scripture (Hebrews 12:5–6; James 4:6). Melito of Sardis, about AD 170, lists "the Proverbs of Solomon, which is also Wisdom" among the books of the Old Testament, and early Christian writers often called Proverbs "all-virtuous Wisdom" (Eusebius, Church History 4.26.14; 4.22.9).

The rabbis remembered a debate. According to the Talmud, "they sought to hide away the book of Proverbs, because its words contradict one another": 26:4 says not to answer a fool according to his folly, and 26:5 says to answer him so. The rabbis resolved it by reading one verse as about matters of Torah and the other about worldly matters, and the book stayed (Bavli Shabbat 30b). Avot de-Rabbi Natan adds that Proverbs, the Song of Songs and Ecclesiastes were once withheld as mere parables, until "the men of Hezekiah" came and interpreted them (Avot de-Rabbi Natan 1).

In Hebrew Bibles Proverbs belongs to the Writings. With Psalms and Job it is one of the three books with a special system of accents for poetry, known by the initials of their Hebrew names, Iyyov, Mishlei, Tehillim, which spell emet, "truth." Later Jewish and Christian writers continued its teaching in the Wisdom of Solomon and Sirach, which Catholic and Orthodox Christians count as Scripture and Jews and most Protestants do not (see the card below).

sections.h: Proverbs in Jewish and Christian teaching
sections.b:
In Jewish life Proverbs has been a school book and a book of prayer. The Mishnah's sayings of the fathers build on it (Mishnah Avot), and the words "To those who grab hold of her she is a tree of life" (3:18) and "Her roads are roads of delight, and every one of her paths is peace" (3:17) are sung when the Torah scroll is returned to the ark, applied to the Torah. On Friday nights many families sing the poem of the woman of strength (31:10–31) before the Sabbath meal. Medieval commentators such as Rashi, Ibn Ezra, Gersonides and Meiri read the book as moral and philosophical training, and the Midrash on Proverbs gathers rabbinic readings verse by verse.

The New Testament quotes Proverbs about a dozen times and echoes it often. Paul calls Christ "the wisdom of God" (1 Corinthians 1:24), and John's prologue and Colossians 1:15–17 describe the Son in words close to Wisdom's in chapter 8. 1 Clement, about AD 96, quotes Wisdom's warning of 1:23–33 at length. The fathers read Wisdom's house of seven pillars and her bread and wine (9:1–5) as pictures of the Church and the Eucharist. The church of Hagia Sophia, "Holy Wisdom," in Constantinople was dedicated to Christ as God's Wisdom. In the fourth century the whole church argued over 8:22 (see the page on chapter 8).

Catholic and Orthodox worship reads Proverbs 8 and 9 on feasts of Christ and of Mary: the Catholic lectionary reads 8:22–31 on Trinity Sunday in one year of its cycle, and Orthodox Vespers for feasts of the Mother of God read 9:1–11. In Protestant churches Proverbs has been above all a book of moral teaching for the young, from the Reformers' catechisms to modern devotional reading of a chapter a day, one for each day of the month.

spec.title: Claude's theory: the son is asked to do what God did first
spec.body: My own reading: the verb qanah, "acquire," ties the father's teaching to Wisdom's account of creation. The father begins by saying that a wise person "will acquire the art of steering" (1:5), and his own father told him, "Acquire wisdom; acquire understanding" (4:5, 7). Then Wisdom says, "The LORD acquired me, the first of his way" (8:22). If the same verb is heard in each place, the son who acquires wisdom is doing on a small scale what the LORD did before the world began: he takes hold of Wisdom first, before his own works, and builds his life by her as the LORD built the world by her (3:19). Commentators note the repeated verb and argue about its meaning in 8:22; reading the chain as a deliberate invitation to imitate the Creator is my suggestion.

reading: Michael V. Fox, Proverbs 1–9 and Proverbs 10–31, Anchor Yale Bible (2000–2009)
The fullest modern commentary, careful on the Hebrew, the Greek and the Egyptian parallels.
Bruce K. Waltke, The Book of Proverbs, 2 vols., NICOT (2004–2005)
A detailed evangelical commentary that defends the book's headings and reads it as a whole.
Roland E. Murphy, Proverbs, Word Biblical Commentary (1998)
A balanced Catholic commentary with good surveys of scholarship and of the book's later readers.
Richard J. Clifford, Proverbs, Old Testament Library (1999)
A compact commentary strong on the ancient Near Eastern background.
A literary translation of Job, Proverbs and Ecclesiastes with brief notes on the poetry.
Claudia V. Camp, Wisdom and the Feminine in the Book of Proverbs (1985)
A study of Lady Wisdom and the women of Proverbs in Israel's social world.

traditions.q: Are the Wisdom of Solomon and Sirach, which continue Proverbs' teaching, part of Scripture?
views: Yes. Both are among the deuterocanonical books that the Council of Trent listed as Scripture in 1546, and the Church reads them in its liturgy, often beside Proverbs 8 and 9.
Yes, as books "worthy to be read" (anagignoskomena) that belong to the Old Testament of the Greek Bible; the Wisdom of Solomon is read with Proverbs at Vespers on many feasts.
Luther printed them in a separate section of his Bible as "Apocrypha: books not held equal to Holy Scripture, but useful and good to read," and Lutheran churches keep that judgment.
The Church "doth read" them "for example of life and instruction of manners; but yet doth it not apply them to establish any doctrine" (Article VI).
No. The Westminster Confession says the Apocrypha "are no part of the canon of the Scripture" and are to be used only like other human writings.
No. Baptist confessions list only the 39 books of the Hebrew Bible as the Old Testament.
No. Most evangelicals accept only the Hebrew canon, though many value the two books as early Jewish witnesses to the idea of Wisdom.
